questions.stem: （第 1 空）
questions.explanation:
【答案】
[ D ] Without词义辨析
【线索】
空前后呼应：自动门 = 不需要触碰
__(1)__ the need to be touched to open or close, automatic doors are essential 提示"自动门"与"触碰需要"之间是排斥关系——正因为不需要触碰才叫"自动"，所以空处应填表达"没有"的介词。
【选项】
A)Through✗方向错：表示"通过/凭借"
Through 表示"凭借某手段"，代入会得到"凭借需要触碰"，与 automatic 的本义相反。
B)Despite✗让步关系不成立
Despite 表示"尽管有……"，代入意味着自动门是"在需要触碰的情况下"仍然必要，与下文 essential in disabled access 形成的肯定语义脱节。
C)Besides✗并列关系不成立
Besides 表示"除……之外（还）"，会承认 "the need to be touched" 是自动门已具备的属性之一，与"自动"互相矛盾。
D)Without✓精准对应 automatic 的定义
Without 直接表达"不需要被触碰"，与主句 automatic doors are essential 同向呼应，把"自动"这一核心特征点了出来。
【验证】
代回后 __(1)__ the need to be touched to open or close, automatic doors are essential in __(2)__ disabled access to buildings 意为"无需触碰即可开关，自动门对无障碍出入至关重要"，逻辑顺畅，与全文"自动门 = 便利"的脉络一致。

questions.stem: （第 2 空）
questions.explanation:
【答案】
[ C ] improving词义辨析
【线索】
并列结构指向"提升/促进"
essential in __(2)__ disabled access to buildings and helping provide general __(3)__ to commercial buildings 中 and 把空 2 的动作与 helping provide 并列，提示空 2 也应是"促成、提升"类正向动词。
【选项】
A)revealing✗义不对："揭示"
revealing 是"使显露"，自动门并非"揭露"无障碍通道，搭配语义不通。
B)demanding✗方向反："要求"带负担色

C)improving✓正向且与 helping provide 同向
improving 表"改善"，与后文 helping provide general __(3)__ 并列，共同表达自动门的两项益处，色彩与逻辑都对。
D)tracing✗义不对："追溯/描绘轮廓"
tracing 与 access 搭配，意为"追踪通行路径"，既不是自动门的作用，也偏离正向语境。
【验证】
代回 essential in __(2)__ disabled access to buildings 得"在改善建筑物无障碍通行方面至关重要"，与全段对自动门价值的肯定吻合。

[ B ] convenience词义辨析
【线索】

questions.stem: （第 4 空）
questions.explanation:
【答案】
[ A ] previously词义辨析
【线索】
1960 是后锚点，六年前的发明 = previously
Self-sliding doors began to emerge as a commercial product in 1960 after being invented six years __(4)__ 已给出"1960 年商业化"和"六年前发明"——after + six years 决定方向是"早于 1960"。
【选项】
A)previously✓精准表达"先于"
previously 与 six years 组合表示"早六年"，把 1960 年商业化与 1954 年发明的时序对得严丝合缝。
B)temporarily✗义不对："暂时"
temporarily 表"暂时性"，与 invented 这一一次性事件冲突，且无法和 six years 形成时序。
C)successively✗义不对："接连地"
successively 表"接连"，需要多次同类事件；发明只发生一次，搭配错。
D)eventually✗方向反："最终"
eventually 表"最终"，会让发明发生在 1960 之后，与 after 提供的时序相反。
【验证】
代回得 after being invented six years __(4)__ = "在六年前被发明之后"，符合"1954 年发明、1960 年商业化"这一阅读常识。

questions.explanation:
【答案】
[ B ] started out固定搭配
【线索】
as a novelty + 后文 use has grown 提示"起步—发展"对照

settled down 多用于人安家、平静下来，与商品起步无关。
D)went by✗义偏："过去/经过"
went by 多用于时间或路过，与 as a novelty feature 搭不上。

代回 They __(5)__ as a novelty feature, but as their use has grown，意为"最初作为新奇事物出现，但随着使用增多……"，与 but 的转折结构完全对应。

questions.material:
Nearly 2,000 years ago, as the Romans began to pull out of Scotland, they left behind a
curious treasure: 10 tons of nails, nearly a million of the things. The nail hoard was
discovered in 1960 in a four-metre-deep pit covered by two metres of gravel.
Why had the Romans buried a million nails? The likely explanation is that the
withdrawal was rushed, and they didn’t want the local Caledonians getting their hands on 10
tons of weapon-grade iron. The Romans buried the nails so deep that they would not be
discovered for almost two millennia.
Later civilisations would value the skilled blacksmith’s labour in a nail even more than
the raw material. As Roma Agrawal explains in her new delightful book Nuts and Bolts,
early 17th-century Virginians would sometimes burn down their homes if they were
planning to relocate. This was an attempt to recover the valuable nails, which could be
reused after sifting the ashes. The idea that one might burn down an entire house just to
reclaim the nails underlines how scarce, costly and valuable the simple-seeming technology
was.
The price of nails fell by 90% between the late 1700s and mid-1900s, as economist
Daniel Sichel points out in a research paper. According to Sichel, although the falling price
of nails was driven partly by cheaper iron and cheaper energy, most of the credit goes to nail
manufacturers who simply found more efficient ways to turn steel into nails.
Nails themselves have changed over the years, but Sichel studied them because they
haven’t changed much. Roman lamps and Roman chariots are very different from LED
strips and sports cars, but Roman nails are still clearly nails. It would be absurd to try to
track the changing price of sports cars since 1695, but to ask the same question of nails
makes perfect sense.
I make no apology for being obsessed by a particular feature of these objects: their
price. I am an economist, after all. After writing two books about the history of inventions,
one thing I’ve learnt is that while it is the enchantingly sophisticated technologies that get all
the hype, it’s the cheap technologies that change the world.
The Gutenberg printing press transformed civilisation not by changing the nature of
writing but by changing its cost — and it would have achieved little without a parallel
collapse in the price of surfaces to write on, thanks to an often-overlooked technology called
paper. Solar panels had few niche uses until they became cheap; now they are transforming
the global energy system.
questions.stem: The Romans buried the nails probably for the sake of ____
questions.explanation:
【答案】
D（细节题）
【判型】
题干 The Romans buried the nails probably for the sake of 指向一个具体历史事件的目的，原文必然有明确解释句，属典型事实细节考查。
【拆句】
题干 The Romans buried the nails probably for the sake of 是一句被「______」截断的陈述句，主干「The Romans buried the nails」+ 状语「for the sake of ___」，副词 probably 仅作软化语气、不影响理解，无陷阱。
【定位】
P2
The likely explanation is that the withdrawal was rushed, and they didn't want the local Caledonians getting their hands on 10 tons of weapon-grade iron.
最可能的解释是，撤退仓促，他们不想让当地的凯尔多尼亚人拿到这 10 吨可作武器原料的铁。
【选项】
A)无中生有
saving them for future use 说留待将来使用，原文从未提罗马人有意保留钉子供日后取用，反而强调埋得极深以致两千年才被发现。
B)无中生有
keeping them from rusting 说防止生锈，原文通篇未涉及锈蚀问题，属凭常识脑补——埋在地下确实可能让人联想到防锈，但文本无此论。
C)张冠李戴
letting them grow in value 说让钉子增值，原文从未提到罗马人埋钉是出于升值动机，钉子升值的话题（P3）发生在后世，与罗马人无关。
D)✓ 正确
they didn't want the local Caledonians getting their hands on 10 tons of weapon-grade iron↔hiding them from the locals
预判「防止当地人拿到铁」与 hiding them from the locals 完全等值，且 D 同时对应「埋得很深 so deep that they would not be discovered」的隐藏动作，锁定 D。

questions.stem: The example of early 17th-century Virginians is used to ____

options.text: highlight the thriftiness of early American colonists.
illustrate the high status of blacksmiths in that period.
contrast the attitudes of different civilisations towards nails.
show the preciousness of nail-making technology at that time.

questions.explanation:
【答案】
D（例证目的题）
【判型】
题干 The example of early 17th-century Virginians is used to 直接用「the example…is used to」明示问例证的功能，是教科书式的例证目的题。
【拆句】
题干 The example of early 17th-century Virginians is used to 是被截断的陈述句，主干「The example...is used to + 不定式」，选项均为不定式短语，与题干补全成完整句即可，无陷阱。
【定位】
P3
The idea that one might burn down an entire house just to reclaim the nails underlines how scarce, costly and valuable the simple-seeming technology was.
「为了回收钉子竟然可能把整栋房子烧掉」这一想法，凸显出这项看似简单的技术当时是何等稀缺、昂贵、珍贵。
【选项】
A)偷换概念
highlight the thriftiness of early American colonists 把作者的论点偷换为「凸显殖民者的节俭」，但原文论点是技术珍贵，节俭只是殖民者为获得珍贵物品的手段，不是被论证的对象。
B)偷换概念
illustrate the high status of blacksmiths in that period 说凸显铁匠的高地位，但原文只说「blacksmith's labour」的价值被看重 Later civilisations would value the skilled blacksmith's labour in a nail even more than the raw material，并未涉及铁匠的社会地位，且例子也非以铁匠为主体。
C)无中生有
contrast the attitudes of different civilisations towards nails 说对比不同文明对钉子的态度，但例子里只出现 17 世纪初弗吉尼亚人这一个文明，并无对比；与罗马人之间也是先后递进而非态度对比。
D)✓ 正确
underlines how scarce, costly and valuable the simple-seeming technology was↔show the preciousness of nail-making technology at that time
预判「凸显造钉技术之珍贵」与 show the preciousness of nail-making technology at that time 在动词、对象、时间上三重对应，锁定 D。

questions.stem: What played the major role in lowering the price of nails after the late 1700s?
questions.explanation:
【答案】
A（细节题）
【判型】
题干 What played the major role in lowering the price of nails after the late 1700s 问的是降价主因这一客观事实，原文有现成对应句，非推断。
【拆句】
题干 What played the major role in lowering the price of nails after the late 1700s 是 What 引导的特殊疑问句，主干「What played the major role」，介词短语「in lowering...」修饰 role，时间状语「after the late 1700s」限定范围，结构平实无陷阱。
【定位】
P4
According to Sichel, although the falling price of nails was driven partly by cheaper iron and cheaper energy, most of the credit goes to nail manufacturers who simply found more efficient ways to turn steel into nails.
根据 Sichel 的研究，虽然钉子价格下降部分得益于铁和能源变便宜，但主要功劳归于钉子制造商，他们找到了把钢转为钉子的更高效方法。
【选项】
A)✓ 正确
nail manufacturers who simply found more efficient ways to turn steel into nails↔Increased productivity
预判「制造效率提升」与 Increased productivity 是同一概念的不同表述（efficiency 与 productivity 在经济学语境下同指投入产出比的优化），锁定 A。
B)偷换概念
Wider use of new energies 把原文 cheaper energy「能源变便宜」偷换为「新能源被更广泛使用」，且原文已明示能源便宜只是次因（partly by），不是 major role。
C)无中生有
Fiercer market competition 说更激烈的市场竞争，原文从未提到竞争，钉子制造商也不是以竞争对手身份出现，而是作为「找到更高效方法」的主体。
D)偷换概念
Reduced cost of raw materials 把原文 cheaper iron「铁变便宜」当作主因，但原文用 although...partly 明示这是次因，主因是制造商的效率提升。

Nearly 2,000 years ago, as the Romans began to pull out of Scotland, they left behind a
curious treasure: 10 tons of nails, nearly a million of the things. The nail hoard was
discovered in 1960 in a four-metre-deep pit covered by two metres of gravel.
Why had the Romans buried a million nails? The likely explanation is that the
withdrawal was rushed, and they didn’t want the local Caledonians getting their hands on 10
tons of weapon-grade iron. The Romans buried the nails so deep that they would not be
discovered for almost two millennia.
Later civilisations would value the skilled blacksmith’s labour in a nail even more than
the raw material. As Roma Agrawal explains in her new delightful book Nuts and Bolts,
early 17th-century Virginians would sometimes burn down their homes if they were
planning to relocate. This was an attempt to recover the valuable nails, which could be
reused after sifting the ashes. The idea that one might burn down an entire house just to
reclaim the nails underlines how scarce, costly and valuable the simple-seeming technology
was.
The price of nails fell by 90% between the late 1700s and mid-1900s, as economist
Daniel Sichel points out in a research paper. According to Sichel, although the falling price
of nails was driven partly by cheaper iron and cheaper energy, most of the credit goes to nail
manufacturers who simply found more efficient ways to turn steel into nails.
Nails themselves have changed over the years, but Sichel studied them because they
haven’t changed much. Roman lamps and Roman chariots are very different from LED
strips and sports cars, but Roman nails are still clearly nails. It would be absurd to try to
track the changing price of sports cars since 1695, but to ask the same question of nails
makes perfect sense.
I make no apology for being obsessed by a particular feature of these objects: their
price. I am an economist, after all. After writing two books about the history of inventions,
one thing I’ve learnt is that while it is the enchantingly sophisticated technologies that get all
the hype, it’s the cheap technologies that change the world.
The Gutenberg printing press transformed civilisation not by changing the nature of
writing but by changing its cost — and it would have achieved little without a parallel
collapse in the price of surfaces to write on, thanks to an often-overlooked technology called
paper. Solar panels had few niche uses until they became cheap; now they are transforming
the global energy system.

【答案】
A（主旨题）
【判型】
题干 Which of the following best summarises the last two paragraphs 明确要求对最后两段做最佳概括，是局部主旨题。
【拆句】
题干 Which of the following best summarises the last two paragraphs 是 Which 引导的特殊疑问句，主干「Which...summarises...paragraphs」，best 作副词修饰 summarises，是常规疑问句结构，无陷阱。
【选项】
A)✓ 正确
it's the cheap technologies that change the world↔Cheap technologies bring about revolutionary change
Solar panels had a few niche uses until they became cheap; now they are transforming the global energy system↔Cheap technologies bring about revolutionary change
预判「便宜技术带来变革」与 Cheap technologies bring about revolutionary change 完全等值，A 同时覆盖第 6 段立论与第 7 段三个例证，锁定 A。
B)偷换概念
Technological innovation is integral to economic success 说技术创新对经济成功不可或缺，但作者在最后两段从未把主语锁定为「creation/创新」，强调的不是「创新」而是「便宜」，且对象是改变世界，不限于经济成功。

Technology defines people's understanding of the world 说技术定义人们对世界的认识，与作者讨论的「技术降价 → 改变世界」毫无对应，「认识论」不是这两段的话题。

Sophisticated technologies develop from small inventions 说复杂技术由小发明发展而来，但作者本意是「便宜技术比高科技更能改变世界」，未谈技术间的演化关系；甚至 enchantingly sophisticated technologies that get all the hype 还把「华丽高科技」放在被贬斥的位置。

questions.material:
Parenting tips obtained from hunter-gatherers in Africa may be the key to bringing up
more contented children, researchers have suggested. The idea is based on studies of
communities such as the Kung of Botswana, where each child is cared for by many adults.
Kung children as young as four will help to look after younger ones and “baby-wearing”, in
which infants are carried in slings, is considered the norm.
According to Dr Nikhil Chaudhary, an evolutionary anthropologist at Cambridge
University, these practices, known as alloparenting, could lead to less anxiety for children
and parents.
Dr Annie Swanepoel, a child psychiatrist, believes that there are ways to incorporate
them into western life. In Germany, one scheme has paired an old people’s home with a
nursery. The residents help to look after the children, an arrangement akin to alloparenting.
Another measure could be encouraging friendships between children in different school
years, to mirror the unsupervised mixed-age playgroups in hunter-gatherer communities.
In a paper published in the Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, researchers
said that the western nuclear family was a recent invention which broke with evolutionary
history. This abrupt shift to an “intensive mothering narrative”, which suggests that mothers
should manage childcare alone, was likely to have been harmful. “Such narratives can lead
to maternal exhaustion and have dangerous consequences,” they wrote.
By contrast, in hunter-gatherer societies adults other than the parents can provide
almost half of a child’s care. One previous study looked at the Efé people of the Democratic
Republic of Congo. It found that infants had an average of 14 alloparents a day by the time
they were 18 weeks old, and were passed between caregivers eight times an hour.
Chaudhary said that parents now have less childcare support from family and social
networks than during most of humans’ evolutionary history, but introducing additional
caregivers could reduce stress and maternal depression, which could have a “knock-on”
benefit to a child’s wellbeing. An infant born to a hunter-gatherer society could have more
than ten caregivers — this contrasts starkly to nursery settings in the UK where regulations
call for a ratio of one carer to four children aged two to three.
While hunter-gatherer children learnt from observation and imitation in mixed-age
playgroups, researchers said that western “instructive teaching”, where pupils are asked to sit
still, may contribute to conditions such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Chaudhary
said that Britain should explore the possibility that older siblings helping their parents
“might also enhance their own social development.”
questions.stem: According to the first two paragraphs, alloparenting refers to the practice of ____

options.text: assigning babies to specific adult caregivers.
teaching parenting skills to older children.
carrying infants around by their parents.

questions.explanation:
【答案】
A（细节题）
【判型】
According to the first two paragraphs, alloparenting refers to the practice of 既限定了原文段落，又用 refers to 直问概念定义，属典型细节题问法。
【拆句】
题干主干是 alloparenting refers to the practice of______，According to the first two paragraphs 是状语修饰整句来源；空位接 the practice of 后的 -ing/名词短语，意味着四个选项要填入一种「做法」。结构平铺直叙，无陷阱。
【定位】
P1
The idea is based on studies of communities such as the Kung of Botswana, where each child is cared for by many adults.
这一观点基于对博茨瓦纳孔人等部落的研究——在这些部落里，每个孩子都由众多成年人共同照料。
【选项】
A)✓ 正确
each child is cared for by many adults↔sharing childcare among community members
Kung children as young as four will help to look after younger ones↔sharing childcare
预判语义「众多成年人共同照护一个孩子」与 sharing childcare among community members 几乎一一对应，故锁 A。
B)偷换概念
assigning babies to specific adult caregivers 中 specific 与原文 many adults（不特定的众多）正相反，把「共担」偷换成「一对一指派」。
C)无中生有
原文 Kung children as young as four will help to look after younger ones 只说大孩子参与照护，并未涉及向他们「教授育儿技巧」；teaching parenting skills to older children 把照护行为与抽象教学混为一谈。

原文中 "baby-wearing", in which infants are carried in slings, is considered the norm 只是 alloparenting 实践的一个例子，而非整体定义；carrying infants around by their parents 还把照护主体限定回 parents，与「共同照护」相悖。

questions.stem: The scheme in Germany is mentioned to illustrate ____

options.text: an attempt to facilitate intergenerational communication.
an approach to integrating alloparenting into western society.
the conventional parenting style in western culture.
the differences between western and African ways of living.

questions.explanation:
【答案】
B（例证目的题）
【判型】
The scheme in Germany is mentioned to illustrate 直接问举例的目的，答题对象是上位论点而非细节。
【拆句】
The scheme in Germany 作主语，is mentioned to illustrate 是被动语态的不定式短语作谓语，空位接宾语；mention 的被动隐含的逻辑主语是「作者」。结构清晰，无陷阱。
【定位】
P3
Dr. Annie Swanepoel, a child psychiatrist, believes that there are ways to incorporate them into western life. In Germany, one scheme has paired an old people's home with a nursery. The residents help to look after the children, an arrangement akin to alloparenting.
儿童精神科医生 Annie Swanepoel 认为，有办法把这些做法融入西方生活。在德国，有一项方案把一所养老院和一所托儿所配对：老人帮忙照看孩子，这种安排类似 alloparenting。

A)答非所问
an attempt to facilitate intergenerational communication 听起来很贴例子表面（老人 + 孩子），但作者举例的真实目的不是促进「代际沟通」，而是把 alloparenting 嵌入西方生活；focus 完全错位。
B)✓ 正确
there are ways to incorporate them into western life↔an approach to integrating alloparenting into western society
an arrangement akin to alloparenting↔alloparenting
预判语义「证明 alloparenting 能引入西方生活」与 an approach to integrating alloparenting into western society 完全对齐，故锁 B。
C)与原文相反
原文德国方案是对常规育儿模式的一次创新尝试；the conventional parenting style in western culture 把它说成「西方常规育儿方式」，与原文意图完全相反——作者举这个例子正是为「打破常规」。
D)偷换概念
the differences between western and African ways of living 把作者论点（如何把非洲式育儿引入西方）改写为「比较两者差异」；原文意在借鉴而非比较，且德国例子本身并未做比较。

options.text: departs from the course of evolution.

questions.explanation:
【答案】
D（细节题）

According to Paragraph 4, the "intensive mothering narrative"______ 用 according to 锁段、用空位等待原文对该术语的客观陈述，属细节题。

P4

Parenting tips obtained from hunter-gatherers in Africa may be the key to bringing up
more contented children, researchers have suggested. The idea is based on studies of
communities such as the Kung of Botswana, where each child is cared for by many adults.
Kung children as young as four will help to look after younger ones and “baby-wearing”, in
which infants are carried in slings, is considered the norm.
According to Dr Nikhil Chaudhary, an evolutionary anthropologist at Cambridge
University, these practices, known as alloparenting, could lead to less anxiety for children
and parents.
Dr Annie Swanepoel, a child psychiatrist, believes that there are ways to incorporate
them into western life. In Germany, one scheme has paired an old people’s home with a
nursery. The residents help to look after the children, an arrangement akin to alloparenting.
Another measure could be encouraging friendships between children in different school
years, to mirror the unsupervised mixed-age playgroups in hunter-gatherer communities.
In a paper published in the Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, researchers
said that the western nuclear family was a recent invention which broke with evolutionary
history. This abrupt shift to an “intensive mothering narrative”, which suggests that mothers
should manage childcare alone, was likely to have been harmful. “Such narratives can lead
to maternal exhaustion and have dangerous consequences,” they wrote.
By contrast, in hunter-gatherer societies adults other than the parents can provide
almost half of a child’s care. One previous study looked at the Efé people of the Democratic
Republic of Congo. It found that infants had an average of 14 alloparents a day by the time
they were 18 weeks old, and were passed between caregivers eight times an hour.
Chaudhary said that parents now have less childcare support from family and social
networks than during most of humans’ evolutionary history, but introducing additional
caregivers could reduce stress and maternal depression, which could have a “knock-on”
benefit to a child’s wellbeing. An infant born to a hunter-gatherer society could have more
than ten caregivers — this contrasts starkly to nursery settings in the UK where regulations
call for a ratio of one carer to four children aged two to three.
While hunter-gatherer children learnt from observation and imitation in mixed-age
playgroups, researchers said that western “instructive teaching”, where pupils are asked to sit
still, may contribute to conditions such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Chaudhary
said that Britain should explore the possibility that older siblings helping their parents
“might also enhance their own social development.”

questions.material:
A Polish digital artist who uses classical painting styles to create dreamy fantasy
landscapes, Greg Rutkowski has made illustrations for games such as Dungeons & Dragons
and Magic: The Gathering. And he’s become a sudden hit in the new world of text-to-image
AI generation.
His distinctive style is now one of the most commonly used prompts in the new open-
source AI art generator Stable Diffusion. The tool, along with other popular image-
generation AI models, allows anyone to create impressive images based on text prompts. For
example, type in “Wizard with sword and a glowing orb of magic fire fights a fierce dragon
Greg Rutkowski,” and the system will produce something that looks not a million miles
away from works in Rutkowski’s style.
But these open-source programs are built by scraping images from the internet, often
without permission and proper attribution to artists. As a result, they are raising tricky
questions about ethics and copyright. And artists like Rutkowski have had enough.
According to the website Lexica, which tracks over 10 million images and prompts
generated by Stable Diffusion, Rutkowski’s name has been used as a prompt around 93,000
times. Rutkowski was initially surprised but thought it might be a good way to reach new
audiences. Then he tried searching for his name to see if a piece he had worked on had been
published. The online search brought back work that had his name attached to it but wasn’t
his.
“It’s been just a month. What about in a year? I probably won’t be able to find my
work out there because the internet will be flooded with AI art,” Rutkowski says. “That’s
concerning.”
Other artists besides Rutkowski have been surprised by the apparent popularity of their
work in text-to-image generators — and some are now fighting back. Karla Ortiz, an
illustrator based in San Francisco who found her work in Stable Diffusion’s data set, has
been raising awareness about the issues around AI art and copyright.
Artists say they risk losing income as people start using AI-generated images based on
copyrighted material for commercial purposes. But it’s also a lot more personal, Ortiz says,
arguing that because art is so closely linked to a person, it could raise data protection and
privacy problems.
“There is a coalition growing within artist industries to figure out how to tackle or
mitigate this,” says Ortiz. The group is in its early days of mobilization, which could involve
pushing for new policies or regulation. One suggestion is that AI models could be trained on
images in the public domain, and AI companies could forge partnerships with museums and
artists, Ortiz says.
questions.stem: What can be learned about Rutkowski from the first two paragraphs?

options.text: He is enthusiastic about using AI models.
He is popular with users of an AI art generator.
He attracts admiration from other illustrators.
He specializes in classical painting digitalization.

questions.explanation:
【答案】
B（细节题）
【判型】
What can be learned about Rutkowski from the first two paragraphs 问的是从指定段落能了解到的关于人物的客观信息，没有 infer/imply 等推断信号词。
【拆句】
句子主干是 What can be learned about Rutkowski——被动语态 "What can be learned" 等于 "What can we learn"，重点是 about 后面的对象 Rutkowski；状语 from the first two paragraphs 限定信息来源。结构平铺直叙，无陷阱。
【定位】
P2
His distinctive style is now one of the most commonly used prompts in the new open-source AI art generator Stable Diffusion.
他独特的画风如今成了新一代开源 AI 绘画生成器 Stable Diffusion 中最常被使用的提示词之一。
【选项】
A)无中生有
前两段只说他的风格被 AI 工具大量复用，从未提及他本人对 AI 模型的态度；说他 enthusiastic about using AI models 完全无文本依据。
B)✓ 正确
one of the most commonly used prompts in the new open-source AI art generator Stable Diffusion↔popular with users of an AI art generator
he's become a sudden hit in the new world of text-to-image AI generation↔popular with users of an AI art generator
预判说他在 AI 生图工具用户中走红，popular with users of an AI art generator 几乎逐词对应这条预判。
C)偷换概念
前两段说他在 Stable Diffusion 用户中走红，从未说他获得 admiration from other illustrators——同行插画师并未在前两段出现。
D)偷换概念
原文只说他 uses classical painting styles to create dreamy fantasy landscapes，是"用古典画风创作幻想风景"，并非 classical painting digitalization（把古典画作数字化）。

questions.stem: The problem with open-source AI art generators is that they ____

options.text: lack flexibility in responding to prompts.
make unauthorized use of online images.

questions.explanation:
【答案】
C（细节题）
【判型】
The problem with open-source AI art generators is that they______ 是补全句式，问的是这些生成器存在的客观问题，是细节题。
【拆句】
主干 The problem with ... is that they ______——"The problem ... is that ..." 是 "主语 is that 表语从句" 结构，that 引导的从句是表语，空白处补充从句的谓语动词及其后内容；代词 they 回指 open-source AI art generators。结构清晰，无陷阱。
【定位】
P3
But these open-source programs are built by scraping images from the Internet, often without permission and proper attribution to artists.
但这些开源程序是通过从互联网抓取图片来构建的，往往没有得到许可，也没有恰当地注明艺术家的署名。
【选项】
A)与原文相反
allows anyone to create impressive images based on text prompts 反而说它能对各类文本提示作出令人印象深刻的回应，与 lack flexibility in responding to prompts 相反。
B)与原文相反
原文 the system will produce something that looks not a million miles away from works in Rutkowski's style 说生成结果与某画家风格高度接近，恰恰是可预测、可模仿的，unpredictable styles 与原文方向相反。
C)✓ 正确
scraping images from the Internet, often without permission and proper attribution to artists↔make unauthorized use of online images
预判中"未经授权"对应 unauthorized，"抓网图"对应 use of online images，直接锁定 C。
D)无中生有
原文谈的是抓取艺术家的画作和未署名问题，从未提及收集用户个人信息；collect user information without consent 是无原文依据的捏造。

questions.stem: After searching online, Rutkowski found ____

options.text: a unique way to reach audiences.
a new method to identify AI images.

questions.explanation:
【答案】
C（细节题）
【判型】
After searching online, Rutkowski found______ 直接问发现了什么客观事物，没有任何推断信号词。
【拆句】
主干 Rutkowski found ______——主语 + 谓语 + 待补宾语；前置 After searching online 是时间状语，约束 found 这个动作发生的时间点。结构简单，无陷阱。

P4
Then he tried searching for his name to see if a piece he had worked on had been published. The online search brought back work that had his name attached to it but wasn't his.

work that had his name attached to it but wasn't his↔AI-generated work bearing his name
预判说他搜到"挂他名却非他作"的画，本文主线是 AI 生图，逻辑链完全指向 AI-generated work bearing his name。

questions.stem: According to Ortiz, AI companies are advised to ____

options.text: campaign for new policies or regulation.
offer their services to public institutions.
strengthen their relationships with AI users.
adopt a different strategy for AI model training.

questions.explanation:
【答案】
D（细节题）
【判型】
According to Ortiz, AI companies are advised to______ 问 Ortiz 给出的具体建议，本质是定位 Ortiz 言论中的一条具体主张。
【拆句】
主干 AI companies are advised to ______——被动语态 "are advised to do sth."，建议的接受方是 AI companies，待补内容是建议的具体动作不定式；前置插入语 According to Ortiz 标明建议发出者。结构清晰，注意被动语态隐藏了建议人，须靠 According to 锁定。
【定位】
P8
One suggestion is that AI models could be trained on images in the public domain, and AI companies could forge partnerships with museums and artists, Ortiz says.
Ortiz 说，一个建议是 AI 模型可以用公共领域的图片进行训练，AI 公司可以与博物馆和艺术家建立合作关系。

A)张冠李戴
原文 which could involve pushing for new policies or regulation 主语 The group（艺术家联盟）才是要推动新政策的一方，不是 AI 公司；campaign for new policies or regulation 把行为方从联盟偷换为 AI 公司。

原文说 AI 公司与博物馆、艺术家建立合作，不是 offer their services to public institutions——"建合作"与"向公共机构提供服务"动作方向和性质完全不同。
C)无中生有

D)✓ 正确

questions.material:
A Polish digital artist who uses classical painting styles to create dreamy fantasy
landscapes, Greg Rutkowski has made illustrations for games such as Dungeons & Dragons
and Magic: The Gathering. And he’s become a sudden hit in the new world of text-to-image
AI generation.
His distinctive style is now one of the most commonly used prompts in the new open-
source AI art generator Stable Diffusion. The tool, along with other popular image-
generation AI models, allows anyone to create impressive images based on text prompts. For
example, type in “Wizard with sword and a glowing orb of magic fire fights a fierce dragon
Greg Rutkowski,” and the system will produce something that looks not a million miles
away from works in Rutkowski’s style.
But these open-source programs are built by scraping images from the internet, often
without permission and proper attribution to artists. As a result, they are raising tricky
questions about ethics and copyright. And artists like Rutkowski have had enough.
According to the website Lexica, which tracks over 10 million images and prompts
generated by Stable Diffusion, Rutkowski’s name has been used as a prompt around 93,000
times. Rutkowski was initially surprised but thought it might be a good way to reach new
audiences. Then he tried searching for his name to see if a piece he had worked on had been
published. The online search brought back work that had his name attached to it but wasn’t
his.
“It’s been just a month. What about in a year? I probably won’t be able to find my
work out there because the internet will be flooded with AI art,” Rutkowski says. “That’s
concerning.”
Other artists besides Rutkowski have been surprised by the apparent popularity of their
work in text-to-image generators — and some are now fighting back. Karla Ortiz, an
illustrator based in San Francisco who found her work in Stable Diffusion’s data set, has
been raising awareness about the issues around AI art and copyright.
Artists say they risk losing income as people start using AI-generated images based on
copyrighted material for commercial purposes. But it’s also a lot more personal, Ortiz says,
arguing that because art is so closely linked to a person, it could raise data protection and
privacy problems.
“There is a coalition growing within artist industries to figure out how to tackle or
mitigate this,” says Ortiz. The group is in its early days of mobilization, which could involve
pushing for new policies or regulation. One suggestion is that AI models could be trained on
images in the public domain, and AI companies could forge partnerships with museums and
artists, Ortiz says.

questions.material:
The miracle of the Chesapeake Bay lies not in its depths, but in the complexity of its
natural construction, the interaction of fresh and saline waters, and the mix of land and water.
The shallows provide homes for hundreds of species while storing floodwaters, filtering
pollutants from water, and protecting nearby communities from potentially destructive storm
surges.
All this was put at great risk late last month, when the U.S. Supreme Court issued a
ruling in an Idaho case that provides the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) far
less authority to regulate wetlands and waterways. Specifically, a 5-4 majority decided that
wetlands protected by the EPA under its Clean Water Act authority must have a “continuous
surface connection” to bodies of water. This narrowing of the regulatory scope was a victory
for builders, mining operators and other commercial interests often at odds with
environmental rules. And it carries “significant repercussions for water quality and flood
control throughout the United States,” as Justice Brett Kavanaugh observed.
In Maryland, the good news is that there are many state laws in place that provide
wetlands protections. But that’s a very shortsighted view, particularly when it comes to the
Chesapeake Bay. The reality is that water, and the pollutants that so often come with it,
don’t respect state boundaries. The Chesapeake draws from a 64,000-square-mile watershed
that extends into Virginia, Pennsylvania, New York, West Virginia, the District of Columbia
and Delaware. Will those jurisdictions extend the same protections now denied under
Sackett v. EPA? Perhaps some, but all? That seems unlikely.
It is too easy, and misleading, to see such court rulings as merely standing up for the
rights of land owners when the consequences can be so dire for their neighbors. And it’s a
reminder that the EPA’s involvement in the Chesapeake Bay Program has long been crucial
as the means to transcend the influence of deep-pocketed special interests in neighboring
states. Pennsylvania farmers, to use one telling example, aren’t thinking about next year’s
blue crab harvest in Maryland when they decide whether to spread animal waste on their
fields, yet the runoff into nearby creeks can have enormous impact downstream.
And so we would call on state lawmakers from Richmond to Albany to consider
reviewing their own wetlands protections and see for themselves the enormous stakes
involved. We can offer them a visit to Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge in Dorchester
County where bald eagles fly over tidal marshes so shallow you could not paddle a boat
across them but teaming with aquatic life. It’s worth the scenic drive.

(41) Hannah
Simply, there are people in Nigeria who cannot travel to the Smithsonian Institution to
see that part of their history and culture represented by the Benin Bronzes. These should be
available to them as part of their cultural heritage and history and as a source of national
pride. There is no good reason that these artifacts should be beyond the ordinary reach of the
educational objectives or inspiration of the generations to which they were left. They serve
no purpose in a museum in the United States or elsewhere except as curious objects. They
cannot be compared to works of art produced for sale which can be passed from hand to
hand and place to place by purchase.
(42) Buck
We know very exact reproductions of artwork can be and are regularly produced.
Perhaps museums and governments might explore some role for the use of nearly exact
reproductions as a means of resolving issues relating to returning works of art and
antiquities. The context of any exhibit is more important to me than whether the object being
displayed is 2000 years old or 2 months old. In many cases the experts have a hard time
agreeing on what is the real object and what is a forgery. Again, the story an exhibit is
trying to tell is what matters. The monetary value of the objects on display is a distant
second place in importance.
(43) Sara
When visiting the Baltimore Museum of Art, I came across a magnificent 15th-century
Chinese sculpture. It inspired me to learn more about the culture that it represented. Artifacts
in museums have the power to inspire, and perhaps spark that need to learn and understand
the nature of their creators. Having said that, I do feel that whatever artifacts find their way
to public museums should, in fact, be sanctioned as having been obtained on loan, legally
purchased, or obtained by treaty. Stealing artifacts from other peoples’ cultures is obscene; it
robs not only the physical objects, but the dignity and spirit of their creators.
(44) Victor
Ancient art that is displayed in foreign countries by all means should be returned to the
original country. The foreign countries have no right to hold back returning the items. I
would ask that the foreign nations and the original country discuss the terms of transfer. Yes,
there is the risk that the original country will not have as good security as do the foreign
countries. But look at what happened to Boston’s Gardner Museum theft in 1990, including
the loss of Rembrandt, Vermeer, Manet, and other masterpieces. Nothing is absolutely safe,
nowhere. And now Climate Change agitators are attacking publicly displayed works in
European museums.
(45) Julia
To those of you in the comments section who are having strong feelings about artifacts
being removed from cities in the US and Britain and returned to their countries of origin, I
would ask you to consider: why do you think Americans have more of a right to easily
access the Benin Bronzes than the people of Nigeria? Why are people who live within a
day’s drive of London entitled to go and see the Elgin Marbles whenever they want, but the
people of Athens aren’t? What intrinsic factors make the West a suitable home for these
artifacts but preclude them from being preserved and displayed by their countries of origin?
If your conclusion is that the West is better able to preserve these artifacts, think about why
you’re assuming that to be true.
A. It is clear that the countries of origin have never been compensated for the stolen artifacts.
B. It is a flawed line of reasoning to argue against returning artifacts to their countries of
origin.
C. Museum visitors can still learn as much from artifacts’ copies after the originals are
returned.
D. Reproductions, even if perfectly made, cannot take the place of the authentic objects.
E. The real value of artifacts can only be recognized in their countries of origin rather than
anywhere else.
F. Ways to get artifacts from other countries must be decent and lawful.
G. Concern over security is no excuse for refusing to return artifacts to their countries of
origin.

questions.material:
“Elephants never forget” — or so they say — and that piece of folklore seems to
have some foundation.
The African savanna elephant, also known as the African bush elephant, is
distributed across 37 African countries. They move between a variety of habitats,
including forests, grasslands, woodlands, wetlands and agricultural land. (46) They
sometimes travel more than sixty miles to find food or water, and are very good at
working out where other elephants are — even when they are out of sight. Using tracking
devices, researchers have shown that they have “remarkable spatial acuity.” When
finding their way to waterholes, they headed off in exactly the right direction, on one
occasion from a distance of roughly thirty miles. What is more, they almost always seem
to choose the nearest waterhole. (47) The researchers are convinced that the elephants
always know precisely where they are in relation to all the resources they need, and can
therefore take shortcuts, as well as following familiar routes.
Although the cues used by African elephants for long-distance navigation are not
yet understood, smell may well play a part.
Elephants are very choosy eaters, but until recently little was known about how they
selected their food. (48) One possibility was that they merely used their eyes and tried
out the plants they found, but that would probably result in a lot of wasted time and
energy, not least because their eyesight is actually not very good.
(49) The volatile chemicals produced by plants can be carried a long way, and they
are very characteristic: Each plant or tree has its own particular odor signature. What is
more, they can be detected even when they are not actually visible. New research
suggests that smell is a crucial factor in guiding elephants — and probably other
herbivores — to the best food resources.
The researchers first established what kinds of plant the elephants preferred either to
eat or avoid when foraging freely. They then set up a “food station” experiment, in which
they gave the elephants a series of choices based only on smell. (50) The experiment
showed that elephants may well use smell to identify patches of trees that are good to eat,
and secondly to assess the quality of the trees within each patch. Free-ranging elephants
presumably also use this information to locate their preferred food.
Their well-developed hippocampal structures may enable elephants, like rats and
people, to construct cognitive maps.

including forests, grasslands, woodlands, wetlands and agricultural land. (46) They
sometimes travel more than sixty miles to find food or water, and are very good at
working out where other elephants are — even when they are out of sight. Using tracking
devices, researchers have shown that they have “remarkable spatial acuity.” When
finding their way to waterholes, they headed off in exactly the right direction, on one
occasion from a distance of roughly thirty miles. What is more, they almost always seem
to choose the nearest waterhole. (47) The researchers are convinced that the elephants
always know precisely where they are in relation to all the resources they need, and can
therefore take shortcuts, as well as following familiar routes.
Although the cues used by African elephants for long-distance navigation are not
yet understood, smell may well play a part.
Elephants are very choosy eaters, but until recently little was known about how they
selected their food. (48) One possibility was that they merely used their eyes and tried
out the plants they found, but that would probably result in a lot of wasted time and
energy, not least because their eyesight is actually not very good.
(49) The volatile chemicals produced by plants can be carried a long way, and they
are very characteristic: Each plant or tree has its own particular odor signature. What is
more, they can be detected even when they are not actually visible. New research
suggests that smell is a crucial factor in guiding elephants — and probably other
herbivores — to the best food resources.
The researchers first established what kinds of plant the elephants preferred either to
eat or avoid when foraging freely. They then set up a “food station” experiment, in which
they gave the elephants a series of choices based only on smell. (50) The experiment
showed that elephants may well use smell to identify patches of trees that are good to eat,
and secondly to assess the quality of the trees within each patch. Free-ranging elephants
presumably also use this information to locate their preferred food.
Their well-developed hippocampal structures may enable elephants, like rats and
people, to construct cognitive maps.

Read the following email from an international student and write a reply.
Write your answer in about 100 words on the ANSWER SHEET.
Do not use your own name in your email; use “Li Ming” instead. (10 points)
Dear Li Ming,
I’ve got a class assignment to make an oral report on an ancient Chinese
scientist, but I’m not sure how to prepare for it. Can you give me some advice?
Thank you for your help.
Yours,
Paul
questions.answer:
Dear Paul,
I'm glad you wrote to me, and I'd be more than happy to help you prepare your oral report.
Here are some suggestions. First, choose one scientist you find interesting, such as Zu Chongzhi or Li Shizhen. Then, look up reliable books and websites to collect facts about his life and major achievements. After that, write a clear outline so that your ideas flow smoothly from one point to the next. Finally, practice reading the report aloud several times until you feel confident and relaxed.
I'm sure your report will be a great success. Good luck!
Yours,
Li Ming

Directions:
Write an essay based on the picture and the chart below. In your essay, you should
1) describe the picture and the chart briefly,
2) interpret the implied meaning, and
3) give your comments.
Write your answer in 160-200 words on the ANSWER SHEET. (20 points)
2020年 2021年 2022年
某市近三年公园数量
（单位：座）
questions.answer:
As is depicted in the picture, five residents are enjoying themselves in a newly built park: two children are running, a couple are chatting, and a delighted man exclaims that the small park near his home is wonderful, with a board reading "Citizen Fitness Area" standing nearby. The accompanying chart reinforces this scene: the number of parks in a certain city climbed steadily from 406 in 2020 to 532 in 2021, and to 670 in 2022.
Simple as they seem, the picture and the chart jointly reveal a heartening trend: our cities are investing more in public green spaces, and such spaces are enriching residents' daily lives. The rising bars are not merely cold figures; behind each of them lie the laughter of children and the leisure of ordinary families. In essence, urban parks bridge material progress and spiritual well-being.
In view of this, I firmly hold that building more parks deserves our applause and support. On the one hand, the government should keep increasing green areas and equip them with fitness facilities. On the other hand, we citizens ought to cherish and protect these shared spaces. Only in this way can our cities grow both greener and happier.
